strengths: Novel task formulation: Personalized distractor generation is well-motivated pedagogically and addresses a real limitation of group-level approaches
Creative methodology: MCTS-based reasoning trajectory recovery with terminal node design effectively captures diverse error patterns including premature reasoning termination
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Five LLMs, multiple datasets, eight baselines, thorough ablation studies, and parameter sensitivity analysis demonstrate rigor
Consistent empirical improvements: Substantial gains across datasets and models, especially on reasoning-intensive tasks (28.6% vs 16.7% on Discrete 40)
Generalization capability: Method works in both personalized and group-level settings, suggesting robustness
Real-world validation: User study provides concrete evidence of improved diagnostic effectiveness (higher error rate, lower abstain rate with personalized distractors)
Well-structured presentation: Clear motivation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2)
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale: Only 100 and 40 students with ~57 past and ~10 test records per student; small scale limits generalizability of findings

Ground truth assumption problem: Primary metric assumes student's selected distractor reliably reflects their misconception, but this is unvalidated; students may select distractors for reasons unrelated to their reasoning (guessing, test anxiety)

Evaluation concerns: (1) Plausibility/Coherence rely on LLM-based metrics that may exhibit bias; (2) No human evaluation of distractor quality beyond limited user study; (3) No validation that recovered trajectories match actual student reasoning; (4) No statistical significance testing
Unvalidated core assumption: Temporal stability of misconceptions within one week is assumed but not empirically validated

MCTS implementation opacity: (1) Mechanism for generating B-1 plausible but incorrect alternatives not explained; (2) Multiple equally plausible trajectories may exist—no evidence MCTS recovers 'the' most plausible one; (3) Parameter choices (B=3, α=0.2) appear arbitrary
Limited user study: Only 10 students (5 per group) with no statistical significance testing; 'None of the above' option could confound results
Reproducibility limitations: All components use black-box LLMs; critical prompts not in main paper; Discrete 40 dataset availability unclear; no code/data release mentioned
Missing technical details: No computational cost analysis; no edge case discussion (few QA records, concept drift); limited error analysis
Domain specificity: Both datasets are math-focused; generalization to other domains (reading, science) unclear
Limited qualitative analysis: Few concrete examples of recovered trajectories; no systematic analysis of misconception types captured vs. missed

strengths: Novel task definition with clear practical motivation: personalized distractor generation addresses a genuine gap in group-level approaches, with compelling examples of how student-specific distractors improve diagnostic effectiveness

Creative technical approach: MCTS-based reasoning trajectory recovery with terminal node design cleverly captures realistic student errors including premature termination; training-free framework is immediately practical

Comprehensive multi-model evaluation: experiments across 5 different LLM architectures (including open-source and proprietary models) provide model-agnostic conclusions; 8 diverse baselines for thorough comparison

Thorough ablation studies and sensitivity analysis: Table 3 demonstrates contribution of each component; Figure 3 shows principled parameter tuning across datasets; results are reproducible across different models

Careful dataset curation: two datasets spanning difficulty levels with documented filtering criteria, ethics review, and informed consent; temporal stability ensured through one-week window constraint

Real-world validation: user study with treatment/control design (Table 5, Figure 4) demonstrates that personalized distractors improve diagnostic effectiveness with higher error rates and lower abstain rates
Generalization to group-level settings: Table 4 shows cross-dataset generalization with better robustness than trained baselines like D-GEN and DiVERT
weaknesses: Problematic accuracy metric and low overall performance: accuracy metric (matching student's actual distractor) is fundamentally limited since multiple different distractors can reflect the same misconception; absolute performance remains low (17.7-32.1% on Eedi 100, 28.6-40.4% on Discrete 40), raising questions about ground truth validity

Severely limited user study: only 10 students (5 per group) is insufficient for statistical inference; no significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple trials reported; single dataset limits generalizability; possible sampling bias

Critical technical details missing: specification of ϕ_concept (concept extraction method, prompts, training data) is unclear despite 3-4% performance impact; ϕ_sum summarization mechanism poorly explained; retrieval procedure in Stage 2 not detailed (concept matching strategy unknown)

Unjustified MCTS parameter choices: tree depth D=5 seems shallow for complex reasoning; B=3 children per node lacks justification; α=0.2 for reward weighting appears arbitrary; most parameter analysis relegated to unavailable appendix

Small datasets with limited diversity: 140 total students (only 40 in Discrete 40) is modest; only math MCQs evaluated with no evidence of generalization to other domains or question types; elementary math limited to basic arithmetic

Untested core assumptions: temporal stability of misconceptions over one-week window never validated; no analysis of learning/correction during the period; method assumes sparse data regime but doesn't test sensitivity to number of past records

Questionable evaluation metrics: LLM-based evaluation (Plausibility, Coherence) using o3-mini has no inter-rater reliability; using LLMs to evaluate other LLMs' reasoning could introduce circular biases; math-verify is domain-specific

Overstated group-level generalization: indirect approach of aggregating personalized predictions may unfairly compare to methods specifically designed for group-level generation; trained baselines may face inherent disadvantages

Insufficient failure analysis: no discussion of concept extraction failures, insufficient data scenarios (2-3 past records), or how curriculum effects impact performance; limited exploration of when method fails

strengths: Novel task formulation with clear motivation: personalized distractor generation addresses a genuine gap in educational assessment where group-level distractors fail to capture individual misconceptions
Creative technical approach: MCTS-based reasoning trajectory reconstruction is well-justified; the distinction between reasoning and terminal nodes elegantly captures premature stopping
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: testing across 5 LLMs, multiple datasets, thorough ablations, human evaluation confirming metric validity, and evaluation of intermediate pipeline components
Strong benchmarking results: consistent improvements across all metrics; particularly effective on reasoning-intensive domains (Discrete_40)

Real-world validation efforts: user study demonstrates treatment group with personalized distractors shows lower abstain rate (0.06 vs 0.14) and meaningful PD rate (0.4), providing concrete evidence of diagnostic effectiveness
Excellent reproducibility documentation: detailed algorithm pseudocode, prompt designs, implementation details, and dataset statistics provided in comprehensive appendix
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: problem motivation well-illustrated (Figure 1), two-stage framework clearly explained (Figure 2), good use of case studies
weaknesses: Critical assumption unvalidated: paper assumes student misconceptions remain stable over one-week periods with no empirical evidence; if this assumption breaks down, the task foundation is undermined

Primary evaluation metric has questionable validity: Accuracy measures whether generated distractor matches student-selected option, but students may select through guessing, careless errors, or factors unrelated to misconceptions; metric conflates matching behavior with revealing true misconceptions

Limited real-world validation: user study with only 30 students is insufficient for strong claims about diagnostic effectiveness; no statistical significance testing; single case study (Figure 4) is anecdotal

Reasoning reconstruction faithfulness unclear: MCTS reconstructs plausible but potentially inaccurate reasoning trajectories; behavioral consistency validation covers only 5 students on 25 questions; risk that distractors based on incorrect reconstructions fail to reveal true misconceptions

Scalability concerns despite claims: main experiments on small subsets (100 and 40 students) due to computational costs; full dataset evaluation compares only against one baseline; MCTS requires multiple LLM calls per node with cumulative cost not quantified

Dataset ground truth validity: Student_1361 uses student-selected options as ground truth, inheriting the same validity issues; temporal windowing (one week) and filtering criteria may introduce biases; restricted to text-only questions with deterministic answers limiting generalizability

Incomplete failure mode analysis: lower accuracy on CP_39 (6.7%) and OS_124 (12.4%) acknowledged but not addressed; bad case analysis identifies incidental mistakes but proposes only future work; no systematic characterization of failure cases

Missing sensitivity analyses: no depth on how performance scales with sparse histories (M ranges 17-63); no analysis of very sparse scenarios (<10 records); hyperparameter selection (B=3, α=0.2, L values) lacks principled justification despite ablations

Limited baseline comparisons at scale: strongest baselines (IO, CoT) compared on one model; no comparison with recent student modeling or knowledge tracing methods that could capture individual differences

Generalization questions: tested primarily on math/technical subjects; applicability to non-technical domains or open-ended questions unclear; framework relies on LLM reasoning capabilities that vary by domain
